claim: The Mtb genome encodes the predicted encapsulin gene Rv0798c/Cfp29.
source: The Mtb genome encodes the predicted encapsulin gene Rv0798c/Cfp29 (Contreras et al., 2014) in a two-gene operon with Rv0799c, the dye-decolorizing peroxidase DyP (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Contreras et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1A showing the operon structure.

claim: Rv0798c/Cfp29 is in a two-gene operon with Rv0799c, the dye-decolorizing peroxidase DyP.
source: The Mtb genome encodes the predicted encapsulin gene Rv0798c/Cfp29 (Contreras et al., 2014) in a two-gene operon with Rv0799c, the dye-decolorizing peroxidase DyP (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A which shows the operon structure.

claim: Overexpression of the predicted Mtb encapsulin gene in Escherichia coli results in the formation of nanocompartment-like structures.
source: Overexpression of the predicted Mtb encapsulin gene in Escherichia coli was previously shown to result in the formation of nanocompartment-like structures (Contreras et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Contreras et al., 2014.

claim: Three potential cargo proteins for the nanocompartment were proposed based on a putative shared encapsulation targeting sequence: DyP, FolB, and BrfB.
source: Three potential cargo proteins for the nanocompartment were proposed based on a putative shared encapsulation targeting sequence: DyP, FolB, and BrfB.
evidence: This is a statement about previous proposals, implicitly citing prior work (Contreras et al., 2014 mentioned in context).

claim: Overexpression of DyP, FolB, or BrfB with Cfp29 in E. coli resulted in encapsulation of each protein.
source: In E. coli, overexpression of each protein with Cfp29 resulted in encapsulation.
evidence: This refers to prior work (Contreras et al., 2014) mentioned in the preceding context.

claim: Cfp29 has been identified as a gene required for growth in mice.
source: A transposon screen has identified Cfp29 as a gene required for growth in mice (Zhang et al., 2013) and Cfp29 has long been known as an immunodominant T cell antigen in both mice and human TB patients (Weldingh and Andersen, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Cfp29 is an immunodominant T cell antigen in both mice and human TB patients.
source: A transposon screen has identified Cfp29 as a gene required for growth in mice (Zhang et al., 2013) and Cfp29 has long been known as an immunodominant T cell antigen in both mice and human TB patients (Weldingh and Andersen, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weldingh and Andersen, 1999.

claim: Heterologous expression of the Mtb nanocompartment operon in E. coli produces icosahedral structures with a diameter of ~25 nm.
source: Fractions containing putative nanocompartments were pooled and imaged using transmission electron microscopy, which revealed the presence of icosahedral structures with the expected diameter of ~25 nm (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Mtb produces nanocompartments under normal laboratory growth conditions.
source: To determine whether Mtb produces nanocompartments under normal laboratory growth conditions, we performed an ultracentrifugation-based nanocompartment isolation strategy using wild-type H37Rv strain bacteria grown to mid-log phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). Mass spectrometry analysis of the nanocompartment fraction identified both the encapsulin protein Cfp29 and the peroxidase DyP (Figure 1D). TEM analysis confirmed the presence of nanocompartment particles ~25 nm in diameter (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1D) and TEM analysis (Figure 1E).

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of nanocompartment fractions from Mtb identified both Cfp29 and DyP.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of the nanocompartment fraction identified both the encapsulin protein Cfp29 and the peroxidase DyP (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rv1762c, a protein of unknown function, was consistently identified in purified nanocompartment preparations from Mtb.
source: Interestingly, Rv1762c, a protein of unknown function, was consistently identified in purified nanocompartment preparations from Mtb (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FolB and BrfB were not identified in nanocompartments from Mtb under normal laboratory growth conditions.
source: We were unable to identify either FolB or BrfB in nanocompartments from Mtb, suggesting that these proteins are not endogenous substrates for encapsulation under normal laboratory growth conditions for Mtb.
evidence: Based on the absence of detection in mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Mtb DyP has increased enzymatic activity in low pH environments, with the greatest efficacy at pH 4.0.
source: Similar to the Vibrio cholerae DyP (Uchida et al., 2015), purified Mtb DyP had increased enzymatic activity in low pH environments, with the greatest efficacy at pH 4.0, the lowest pH tested (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by peroxidase activity assay data shown in Figure 1F and comparison to V. cholerae DyP cited from Uchida et al., 2015.

claim: Encapsulated DyP has the highest activity at pH ~4.0.
source: Similar to free DyP, the encapsulated enzyme had the highest activity at pH ~4.0 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by peroxidase activity assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mtb nanocompartments are stable and functional under acid stress conditions that mimic the host lysosomal environment.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate the stability and functionality of Mtb nanocompartments under acid stress, a condition that mimics the host lysosomal environment.
evidence: Inferred from the activity assays at low pH (Figures 1F and 1G).

claim: Mtb DyP functions as a bona fide dye-decolorizing peroxidase.
source: The Mtb DyP protein was previously shown to function as a bona fide dye-decolorizing peroxidase (Contreras et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Contreras et al., 2014.

claim: Peroxidases often participate in defense against oxidative stress because they consume H2O2.
source: Because peroxidases consume H2O2, they often participate in defense against oxidative stress (Mishra and Imlay, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mishra and Imlay, 2012.

claim: Macrophages and neutrophils initiate an oxidative burst that exposes Mtb to H2O2 during infection.
source: During macrophage infection, the phagocytes initiate an oxidative burst that exposes Mtb to H2O2 (El-Benna et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to El-Benna et al., 2009.

claim: Δoperon mutants cannot produce viable nanocompartments.
source: Lysates from Δoperon mutants were used for nanocompartment purification (data not shown) and western blot analysis using an antibody for Cfp29 as a probe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). Data from these analyses revealed that Δoperon mutants cannot produce viable nanocompartments.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DyP::Tn mutants lacking DyP nanocompartments are more susceptible to H2O2 than wild-type bacteria.
source: Mutants lacking DyP nanocompartments were more susceptible to H2O2 when compared with wild-type bacteria as measured by OD600 (Figure 2A) and by plating for colony-forming units (CFU) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by OD600 measurements (Figure 2A) and CFU enumeration (Figure 2B).

claim: Wild-type Mtb can withstand exposure to H2O2 at pH 4.5 for 3 days without significant decrease in bacterial numbers.
source: Wild-type Mtb was able to withstand these conditions and did not significantly decrease in number over a 3-day exposure period (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Δoperon mutants are resistant to acid stress or oxidative stress individually, but are highly susceptible to H2O2 at pH 4.5.
source: In contrast, the Δoperon mutant was resistant to each stressor individually, but was highly susceptible to H2O2 at pH 4.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DyP-containing nanocompartments are required to protect bacteria from oxidative stress at low pH.
source: Thus, DyP-containing nanocompartments are required to protect bacteria from oxidative stress at low pH.
evidence: Inferred from the susceptibility of Δoperon mutants to combined H2O2 and pH 4.5 stress (Figure 2C).

claim: Expression of Cfp29 alone in DyP::Tn mutants results in the formation of empty nanocompartment structures.
source: As expected, expression of DyP did not restore production of nanocompartments, whereas expression of Cfp29 alone resulted in the formation of empty nanocompartment structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Coexpression of both Cfp29 and DyP in DyP::Tn mutants results in the formation of DyP-containing nanocompartments.
source: Coexpression of both proteins resulted in the formation of DyP-containing nanocompartments in the DyP::Tn mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Complementation with unencapsulated DyP alone confers almost wild-type levels of resistance to oxidative and acid stress.
source: Complementation by overexpression of unencapsulated DyP was sufficient to confer almost wild-type levels of resistance to oxidative and acid stress (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Complementation with both Cfp29 and DyP results in enhanced resistance to oxidative and acid stress compared to DyP alone.
source: However, complementation with both Cfp29 and DyP resulted in enhanced resistance to these stressors when compared to mutants complemented with DyP alone (Figure 2D), suggesting that encapsulation of DyP enhances its function.
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Encapsulation of DyP enhances its function in protecting bacteria from oxidative and acid stress.
source: However, complementation with both Cfp29 and DyP resulted in enhanced resistance to these stressors when compared to mutants complemented with DyP alone (Figure 2D), suggesting that encapsulation of DyP enhances its function.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of complementation with DyP alone versus DyP plus Cfp29 (Figure 2D).

claim: Deletion of Cfp29 results in an ~0.5 log decrease in bacterial viability after 3 days of exposure to H2O2 at pH 4.5.
source: Deletion of Cfp29 resulted in an ~0.5 log decrease in bacterial viability after 3 days of exposure to H2O2 at pH 4.5, confirming that encapsulation of the peroxidase in the shell protein is important for full protection (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Encapsulation of DyP in the Cfp29 shell protein is important for full protection against oxidative stress at low pH.
source: Deletion of Cfp29 resulted in an ~0.5 log decrease in bacterial viability after 3 days of exposure to H2O2 at pH 4.5, confirming that encapsulation of the peroxidase in the shell protein is important for full protection (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from the attenuation of Δcfp29 mutants (Figure 2E).

claim: Δoperon mutants have an intracellular environment at baseline that is more oxidizing than wild-type bacteria exposed to H2O2.
source: Remarkably, the Δoperon mutant had an intracellular environment at baseline that was more oxidizing than wild-type bacteria exposed to H2O2 (Figure 2G), indicating a failure of redox homeostasis in mutants lacking the DyP encapsulin system.
evidence: Supported by Mrx1-roGFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mutants lacking DyP-containing nanocompartments exhibit significant dysregulation of redox homeostasis.
source: Thus, mutants lacking DyP-containing nanocompartments exhibit significant dysregulation of redox homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the redox measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Of the 18 putative enzymes encoded by Mtb that could be involved in oxidative defense, only DyP and KatG are required for survival in H2O2 at pH 4.5.
source: These data revealed that of the 18 putative enzymes encoded by Mtb that could be involved in oxidative defense, including peroxidases, catalases, and superoxide dismutases, only two genes were required for survival in the culture conditions—DyP and KatG (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Tn-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: KatG encodes a catalase-peroxidase that is important for defense against oxidative stress in the host.
source: KatG encodes a catalase-peroxidase that is important for defense against oxidative stress in the host (Li et al., 1998; Pym et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 1998 and Pym et al., 2002.

claim: KatG is required for activation of isoniazid (INH).
source: Coincidentally, KatG is also required for activation of isoniazid (INH), a central component of anti-TB therapy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in TB research.

claim: Approximately 10% of TB cases are caused by INH-resistant bacteria, many of which have loss-of-function mutations in KatG.
source: Approximately 10% of TB cases are caused by INH-resistant bacteria, many of which have loss-of-function mutations in KatG (Seifert et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seifert et al., 2015.

claim: KatG variants that do not activate INH often display a concomitant decrease in peroxidase and catalase activity.
source: Importantly, KatG variants that do not activate INH often display a concomitant decrease in peroxidase and catalase activity (DeVito and Morris, 2003; Mo et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeVito and Morris, 2003; Mo et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2003.

claim: Mutants involved in lipid or cholesterol metabolism were attenuated when exposed to H2O2 at pH 4.5.
source: In the Tn-seq data, we observed that mutants involved in lipid or cholesterol metabolism were also attenuated when exposed to H2O2 at pH 4.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Tn-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutants containing transposon insertions in three independent subunits of the Mce1 complex were susceptible to oxidative stress under acidic conditions.
source: In particular, mutants containing transposon insertions in three independent subunits of the Mce1 complex, which is required for import of fatty acids (Nazarova et al., 2019), were susceptible to oxidative stress under acidic conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Tn-seq data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Nazarova et al., 2019.

claim: The Mce1 complex is required for import of fatty acids.
source: In particular, mutants containing transposon insertions in three independent subunits of the Mce1 complex, which is required for import of fatty acids (Nazarova et al., 2019), were susceptible to oxidative stress under acidic conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2019.

claim: In the absence of fatty acids (Sauton's broth), Δoperon mutants persist to the same degree as wild-type bacteria when exposed to acid and oxidative stress.
source: We therefore tested whether fatty acids are required for the susceptibility of Δoperon mutants using exposure to acid and oxidative stress in Sauton's broth, a minimal medium that lacks BSA, and found that in the absence of fatty acids the Δoperon mutants persisted to the same degree as wild-type bacteria (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of BSA-bound lipids, Δoperon mutants are not susceptible to oxidative stress at low pH.
source: In the absence of BSA-bound lipids, we found that the Δoperon mutant was not susceptible to oxidative stress at low pH (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reconstitution of fatty acid-free medium with oleic acid restores toxicity to nanocompartment mutants under conditions of acid and oxidative stress.
source: Reconstitution of fatty acid-free medium with oleic acid restored toxicity to nanocompartment mutants under conditions of acid and oxidative stress (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The intracellular pH of wild-type Mtb drops from ~pH 7.5 to ~pH 6.2 in acidified medium, and this decrease is dependent on the presence of albumin-bound fatty acids.
source: Interestingly, in acidified medium we found that the intracellular pH of wild-type bacteria dropped from ~pH 7.5 to ~pH 6.2, and this decrease was dependent on the presence of albumin-bound fatty acids (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by intrabacterial pH measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The cytosolic pH of Mtb drops significantly during acid exposure.
source: These data confirm published results demonstrating that the cytosolic pH of Mtb drops significantly during acid exposure (Vandal et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vandal et al., 2008 and the current study's pH measurements (Figure 3E).

claim: The Δoperon strain is attenuated for growth in murine bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: We found that the Δoperon strain was consistently attenuated for growth in murine bone marrow-derived macrophages (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data from macrophage infections shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DyP::Tn mutants show attenuated growth in macrophages.
source: However, to confirm that the phenotype of the mutants in macrophages is due to the loss of the two-gene encapsulin operon, we repeated the experiment with the independently derived Dyp:Tn mutant and also observed attenuated growth in macrophages across repeated experiments (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data from macrophage infections shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutants lacking the DyP nanocompartment are sensitive to concentrations of PZA that do not impact growth of wild-type bacteria.
source: We found that mutants lacking the DyP nanocompartment were sensitive to concentrations of PZA that did not impact growth of the wild-type bacteria (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Δoperon mutants are significantly more susceptible to treatment with PZA in vivo.
source: However, Δoperon mutants were significantly more susceptible to treatment with PZA in vivo (Figure 4D), demonstrating that the DyP encapsulin operon is required for endogenous resistance to PZA treatment.
evidence: Supported by CFU enumeration data from mouse infections shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The DyP encapsulin operon is required for endogenous resistance to PZA treatment.
source: However, Δoperon mutants were significantly more susceptible to treatment with PZA in vivo (Figure 4D), demonstrating that the DyP encapsulin operon is required for endogenous resistance to PZA treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the increased susceptibility of Δoperon mutants to PZA in vivo (Figure 4D).

claim: This is the first evidence that encapsulin systems contribute to oxidative stress resistance in a bacterial pathogen.
source: By demonstrating that the encapsulin system is important for resisting oxidative stress at low pH, we provide the first evidence that encapsulin systems contribute to oxidative stress in a bacterial pathogen, and only the second demonstration of a functional encapsulin system in any species.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claim: This is only the second demonstration of a functional encapsulin system in any species.
source: By demonstrating that the encapsulin system is important for resisting oxidative stress at low pH, we provide the first evidence that encapsulin systems contribute to oxidative stress in a bacterial pathogen, and only the second demonstration of a functional encapsulin system in any species.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claim: The protein shell encapsulating DyP enhances its function in vivo.
source: Furthermore, we expand our understanding of the importance of encapsulation in enzyme function by demonstrating that the protein shell encapsulating DyP enhances its function in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from complementation experiments showing enhanced protection with encapsulated DyP (Figure 2D, 2E, 2F).

claim: The DyP nanocompartment system is essential for the ability of Mtb to grow in host macrophages.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the DyP nanocompartment system is essential for the ability of Mtb to grow in host macrophages and to resist killing by the antibiotic PZA.
evidence: Supported by macrophage infection data (Figures 4A and 4B).

claim: The DyP nanocompartment system is essential for Mtb to resist killing by the antibiotic PZA.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the DyP nanocompartment system is essential for the ability of Mtb to grow in host macrophages and to resist killing by the antibiotic PZA.
evidence: Supported by PZA susceptibility data (Figures 4C and 4D).

claim: These findings are the first demonstration that a nanocompartment system is important for virulence in any bacterial pathogen.
source: These findings are the first demonstration that a nanocompartment system is important for virulence in any bacterial pathogen.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claim: Bacterial microcompartments and nanocompartments consist of a porous protein shell that surrounds enzymatic proteins.
source: Rather than using a lipid membrane for compartmentalization, both bacterial microcompartments and nanocompartments consist of a porous protein shell that surrounds enzymatic proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial compartments.

claim: Bacterial microcompartments that enable utilization of ethanolamine and 1,2 propane diol have been implicated in pathogenesis of E. coli and Salmonella enterica, respectively.
source: Bacterial microcompartments that enable utilization of specialized nutrients including ethanolamine and 1,2 propane diol have previously been implicated in pathogenesis of E. coli and Salmonella enterica, respectively (Jakobson and Tullman-Ercek, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jakobson and Tullman-Ercek, 2016.

claim: Nanocompartments are 10 times smaller than a typical bacterial microcompartment.
source: Nanocompartments, which are 10 times smaller than a typical bacterial microcompartment, have been identified bioinformatically in over 900 bacterial species; however, very few studies have addressed the role that nanocompartments play in bacterial physiology.
evidence: This is a comparison based on known structural characteristics.

claim: Nanocompartments have been identified bioinformatically in over 900 bacterial species.
source: Nanocompartments, which are 10 times smaller than a typical bacterial microcompartment, have been identified bioinformatically in over 900 bacterial species; however, very few studies have addressed the role that nanocompartments play in bacterial physiology.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analyses cited elsewhere in the manuscript (Giessen and Silver, 2017).

claim: The only nanocompartment shown to be important for survival under conditions of stress is the ferritin-like protein containing compartment in M. xanthus, which is required for resistance to H2O2.
source: However, the only nanocompartment that has been shown to be important for survival under conditions of stress is the ferritin-like protein containing compartment in M. xanthus, which is required for resistance to H2O2 (McHugh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to McHugh et al., 2014.

claim: Of the three potential cargo proteins (DyP, FolB, BrfB), only DyP was identified in encapsulin systems purified from logarithmically growing Mtb bacteria.
source: Here, we show for the first time that Mtb produces this nanocompartment. However, of the three potential cargo proteins, only DyP was identified in encapsulin systems purified from logarithmically growing bacteria.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1D).

claim: Encapsulin systems have been shown to confer stability to the enzymatic cargo under harsh conditions, including heat and protease exposure.
source: Intriguingly, encapsulin systems have been shown to confer stability to the enzymatic cargo under harsh conditions, including heat and protease exposure (Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: Cfp29 was originally identified as a component of short-term culture filtrate present in broth of growing cells.
source: Cfp29 was originally identified as a component of short-term culture filtrate present in broth of growing cells, leading to the supposition that this protein is secreted (Rosenkrands et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenkrands et al., 1998.

claim: It is unlikely that a structure the size of a ribosome (nanocompartment) could be actively secreted.
source: Given that nanocompartments spontaneously assemble inside cells (Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Nichols et al., 2017; Snijder et al., 2016), it is unlikely that a structure the size of a ribosome could be secreted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size of nanocompartments and citations about their assembly (Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Nichols et al., 2017; Snijder et al., 2016).

claim: Nanocompartments released from dying cells in vivo could continue to provide defense against oxidative stress for the surviving bacteria.
source: Taken together, these data suggest the intriguing possibility that nanocompartments released from dying cells in vivo could continue to provide defense against oxidative stress for the surviving bacteria.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the stability of nanocompartments.

claim: Only two peroxidases, KatG and DyP, are required for survival in the presence of H2O2 at pH 4.5.
source: We found that only two peroxidases, KatG and DyP, are required for survival in the presence of H2O2 at pH 4.5.
evidence: Supported by Tn-seq data (Figure 3A).

claim: KatG and DyP may have redundant function in vivo.
source: These findings raise the possibility that these peroxidases have redundant function in vivo, possibly explaining the lack of attenuation we observed in Δoperon mutants in BALB/C mice at 35 days post infection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the Tn-seq results and mouse infection data.

claim: Many KatG mutants that fail to activate INH are also defective for catalase activity.
source: Importantly, many KatG mutants that fail to activate INH are also defective for catalase activity (DeVito and Morris, 2003; Mo et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeVito and Morris, 2003; Mo et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2003.

claim: The DyP nanocompartment system could partially compensate for a loss of KatG catalase activity, enabling drug resistant mutants to survive in vivo.
source: This raises the possibility that the DyP nanocompartment system could partially compensate for a loss of KatG catalase activity, enabling these drug resistant mutants to survive in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the redundancy of KatG and DyP.

claim: The DyP encapsulin system may limit the efficacy of PZA treatment of patients.
source: Thus, we predict that this encapsulin system may limit the efficacy of PZA treatment of patients.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the PZA susceptibility data (Figures 4C and 4D).

claim: Mtb is highly resistant to oxidative stress, enabling the bacterium to survive within macrophages and neutrophils and establish chronic infection.
source: Importantly, Mtb is highly resistant to oxidative stress, enabling the bacterium to survive within macrophages and neutrophils and establish chronic infection (Chan et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 1992.

claim: Macrophages and neutrophils unleash a respiratory burst that leads to the rapid release of ROS that kill and degrade most microbes.
source: Upon phagocytosis of a pathogen, macrophages and neutrophils unleash a potent microbicidal arsenal, including a respiratory burst that leads to the rapid release of ROS that kill and degrade most microbes (El-Benna et al., 2009; Nathan, 2006; Segal, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to El-Benna et al., 2009; Nathan, 2006; Segal, 2005.

claim: The production of ROS is initiated when NADPH oxidase assembles on pathogen-containing phagosomes.
source: The production of ROS is initiated when NADPH oxidase assembles on pathogen-containing phagosomes and initiates a series of reactions that produce superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hyperchlorous acid, lipid peroxides, and other toxic reactive molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the respiratory burst.

claim: DyP enzymes are unique amongst peroxidases in that some family members have optimal activity at pH 4–5.
source: DyP enzymes are unique amongst peroxidases in that some family members have been shown to have optimal activity at pH 4–5 (Brown et al., 2012; Singh and Eltis, 2015; Uchida et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2012; Singh and Eltis, 2015; Uchida et al., 2015.

claim: DyP is the only Mtb peroxidase predicted to be packaged inside a proteinaceous organelle known as a bacterial nanocompartment.
source: Furthermore, DyP is the only Mtb peroxidase predicted to be packaged inside a proteinaceous organelle known as a bacterial nanocompartment (Contreras et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Contreras et al., 2014.

claim: Characterized nanocompartments are proteinaceous shells that are 24–45 nm in diameter and comprised of 60–240 subunits of a single protomer.
source: Characterized nanocompartments are proteinaceous shells that are 24–45 nm in diameter and comprised of 60–240 subunits of a single protomer (Giessen et al., 2019; Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Giessen et al., 2019 and Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: Putative encapsulin systems have been identified in >900 bacterial and archaeal genomes.
source: Although putative encapsulin systems have been identified in >900 bacterial and archaeal genomes (Giessen and Silver, 2017; Nichols et al., 2020), very little is known about their physiological function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Giessen and Silver, 2017 and Nichols et al., 2020.

claim: Based on genomic organization, encapsulin systems are often predicted to compartmentalize enzymes involved in oxidative stress defense, iron storage, and anaerobic ammonium oxidation.
source: Based on genomic organization, encapsulin systems are often predicted to compartmentalize enzymes involved in oxidative stress defense, iron storage, and anaerobic ammonium oxidation (Giessen and Silver, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giessen and Silver, 2017.

claim: The function of an encapsulin system has only ever been demonstrated in a single bacterial species, Myxococcus xanthus.
source: However, the function of an encapsulin system has only ever been demonstrated in a single bacterial species, Myxococcus xanthus (McHugh et al., 2014), and the physiological role of nanocompartments is largely unexplored.
evidence: Supported by citation to McHugh et al., 2014.

claim: The ability to tolerate low pH is required for Mtb survival in both infected macrophages and mice.
source: During infection, Mtb bacilli encounter the low pH of the phagolysosome and the ability to tolerate low pH is required for Mtb survival in both infected macrophages and mice (Vandal et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vandal et al., 2008.

claim: Mtb granulomas are rich in free fatty acids.
source: Mtb biology is highly linked to lipid biology; Mtb granulomas are rich in free fatty acids (Kim et al., 2010) and the bacteria utilize lipids as a source of nutrition both during macrophage infection ex vivo and growth in vivo (Marrero et al., 2010; Russell, 2011; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Mtb utilizes lipids as a source of nutrition both during macrophage infection ex vivo and growth in vivo.
source: Mtb biology is highly linked to lipid biology; Mtb granulomas are rich in free fatty acids (Kim et al., 2010) and the bacteria utilize lipids as a source of nutrition both during macrophage infection ex vivo and growth in vivo (Marrero et al., 2010; Russell, 2011; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marrero et al., 2010; Russell, 2011; Russell et al., 2019.

claim: PZA is most effective in low pH environments, such as the phagolysosome.
source: One of the antibiotics used to treat TB infection, PZA, is most effective in low pH environments, such as the phagolysosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PZA.

claim: PZA is thought to disrupt the cell wall of Mtb, which leads to acidification of the bacterial cytosol.
source: PZA is thought to disrupt the cell wall of Mtb, which leads to acidification of the bacterial cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of PZA.

claim: The pH of necrotic lung cavities in human TB patients is ~5.5.
source: A recent study in human TB patients demonstrated that the pH of necrotic lung cavities is ~5.5, a finding that may also explain the efficacy of PZA in treating Mtb infection (Kempker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kempker et al., 2017.

claim: Nanocompartments spontaneously assemble inside cells.
source: Given that nanocompartments spontaneously assemble inside cells (Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Nichols et al., 2017; Snijder et al., 2016), it is unlikely that a structure the size of a ribosome could be secreted.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Nichols et al., 2017; Snijder et al., 2016.

claim: Nanocompartment structures are remarkably stable and resistant to proteolysis/degradation.
source: However, nanocompartment structures are remarkably stable and it is possible that nanocompartments released from dying bacteria accumulate in culture as they are highly resistant to proteolysis/degradation (Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016; Nichols et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cassidy-Amstutz et al., 2016 and Nichols et al., 2017.

claim: Δoperon mutants were not attenuated compared to wild-type bacteria in BALB/C mouse lungs at 35 days post infection.
source: We did not find that Δoperon mutants were more attenuated than wild-type bacteria in mouse lungs at 35 days post infection, at least under the conditions examined.
evidence: Supported by mouse infection data (Figure 4D).

claim: The Tn-seq screen that identified Cfp29 as required for growth in mouse lungs used the C57BL/6 strain.
source: It is also possible that Δoperon mutants are not attenuated at this timepoint in BALB/C mice as the Tn-seq screen that previously identified Cfp29 as being required for growth in mouse lungs used the C57BL/6 strain (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Cfp29 lacks a secretory signal sequence.
source: As Cfp29 lacks a secretory signal sequence and is part of a large macromolecular complex, it is unclear how a nanocompartment could be actively secreted.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of Cfp29.

claim: Cfp29 is part of a large macromolecular complex.
source: As Cfp29 lacks a secretory signal sequence and is part of a large macromolecular complex, it is unclear how a nanocompartment could be actively secreted.
evidence: This is based on the structural characterization of nanocompartments.

claim: The extreme stability of nanocompartments may partially explain why Cfp29 is a known immunodominant antigen for T cells.
source: Indeed, this stability may partially explain why Cfp29 is a known immunodominant antigen for T cells (Rosenkrands et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the stability of nanocompartments and citation to Rosenkrands et al., 1998.

claim: Standard Mtb culture medium (7H9) contains bovine serum albumin (BSA).
source: The standard Mtb culture medium, 7H9, contains bovine serum albumin (BSA), which has binding sites for fatty acids and may also serve as a cholesterol shuttle in serum (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2013; van der Vusse, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about 7H9 medium composition.

claim: BSA has binding sites for fatty acids and may serve as a cholesterol shuttle in serum.
source: The standard Mtb culture medium, 7H9, contains bovine serum albumin (BSA), which has binding sites for fatty acids and may also serve as a cholesterol shuttle in serum (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2013; van der Vusse, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2013 and van der Vusse, 2009.

claim: A lower cytosolic pH would possibly impair the function of many other bacterial enzymes important for resisting oxidative stress.
source: A lower cytosolic pH would possibly impair the function of many other bacterial enzymes important for resisting oxidative stress and place increasing importance on enzymes that can function in acidic environments, such as DyP (Uchida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the pH measurements (Figure 3E) and citation to Uchida et al., 2015.
